Costs 29 min

The lift was best in the middle of the band

Split into thirds between 2 053 m and 3 715 m, your climbs averaged +0.78, +1.39 and +0.88 m/s, over 29, 33 and 26 minutes of circling. The top 554 m gave +0.88.

480 mMedian height over the ground directly beneath youThe launch and the landing are left out, or both would win by being on the ground.
6 of 13Climbs began over ground catching more sun than the slopes around itOf the 13 climbs that started over sloping ground. They stayed on ESE-facing ground from 12:07:30 to 15:19:14 rather than following the sun round.
6 of 13Climbs faced within 60° of the measured wind — where ridge lift would beA climb is called ridge only when the slope, the wind and your distance from it all agree; see the Lift column.

How the air was used

Time1 h 27 m climbing across 13 thermals, 1 h 31 m gliding, and 40 m 22 s that was neither. That last part is 9 min of straight sink, 9 min turning without climbing and 23 min of rising air no phase claimed — a net 455 m gained over the whole of it. The climbs and glides account for 82% of airtime; the rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

  • Climbing 1 h 27
  • Gliding 1 h 31
  • Sinking straight 9 min
  • Turning, no climb 9 min
  • Drifting up 23 min

Debrief

Costs 161 min

You spent 161 of your 205 min circling in the day's weaker climbs

27 of your climbs averaged under +2.06 m/s, on a day whose best gave +4.11.

16:03:16

Costs 982 m

Your lowest was 280 m above the valley floor

That was at 13:21:17, and you climbed out of it. For most of the flight you had about 1 262 m above the valley floor (the lowest ground within 2 km). Launch and the glide out to land are left out of this, or they would win every time.

13:21:17

Costs 17 min

You left the day's best climb 418 m below the height you later reached

Climb 12 was running at +4.11 m/s when you left it at 1 872 m. Later in the flight you were at 2 290 m. The next climb took 17 min to find and gave +0.81 m/s.

How the air was used

Time4 h 03 m climbing across 52 thermals, 5 h 49 m gliding, and 1 h 38 m that was neither. That last part is 28 min of straight sink, 13 min turning without climbing and 58 min of rising air no phase claimed — a net 1287 m gained over the whole of it. The climbs and glides account for 86% of airtime; the rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

  • Climbing 4 h 03
  • Gliding 5 h 50
  • Sinking straight 28 min
  • Turning, no climb 13 min
  • Drifting up 58 min

Lift you sat inEvery second spent circling, sorted into half-metre climb-rate buckets. The tallest bar is the climb rate you spent the most time in — not the best one you found. Bars left of zero are time spent turning in sink; the right-hand tail is the cores.

Mostly +2.2 m/s, best sustained about +6 m/s, 5% of the circling in sink

Wind by heightOne point per climb, from circle drift, numbered as in the climbs table and so in the order flown; the first and last carry their clock time, and hovering any point gives the rest. Height is where the climb was worked; the tail points downwind. The model profile for the day is drawn behind them as a check.

2.7 m/s in the lower climbs against 4.4 m/s in the higher ones — 1.7 m/s stronger with height.

  • Measured from circle drift
  • Model profile for the day

The air that dayERA5 reanalysis, surface only over the middle of the course line, valid 2026-06-16 09:00 UTC, fetched once and embedded. A model's analysis, not a radiosonde ascent: treat the ceilings as ±100 m and the winds as indicative.

16 °CSurfaceDew point -5 °C, a spread of 21 K.
6 318 mCloudbaseThe surface air lifted until its 21 K spread closes.
6 241 mBoundary layerAs high as the day's heating reaches.

No sounding for this dateThe reanalysis archive serves surface fields for any past day but returns nothing on pressure levels, so the sounding and the wind comparison are missing here. Flights from the last two months get the full profile.

tracklog viewer

Your own tracks

Read in this page

Nothing is uploaded: the file is parsed and analysed here, and gets the same write-up as the flights above. Each track you add gets its own tab, and the × on a tab removes that flight again.

.igc preferred · or drag them here · .kml and .kmz also read

A KMZ downloaded from a scoring site is usually reduced to 500 points — every few minutes on a long flight. Distances, height gained and turn counts are all measured along the track, so they come out low, and turns cannot be counted at all. The IGC your instrument recorded is the file to use.

TaskPress Draw a task, then click the map to drop turnpoints; drag, pinch and twist still move the view. The route is scored as XContest would and checked against every zone it crosses.

A plan, not a clearance.Scored with the same rules as the flight report: every side at least 28% of the perimeter for FAI, a closing gap under 20% of it for a closed course, multipliers 1 / 1.2 / 1.4. With ČPP chosen, the Czech cup's: closing under 5%, and in the Central European zone 1 / 1.8 / 2.2 (rules). Airspace is drawn for Czechia only.

LayersEverything openAIP carries over Czechia, plus what no published source draws: the traffic circuit at 157 fields and ultralight strips. A paraglider may fly inside an aerodrome zone but must stay out of its circuit, and no instrument draws the circuit. Hover a zone for its name and limits. Each zone is the box it really is — floor to ceiling — so drag with the right button to tilt and see what sits over what. The vertical is exaggerated five times, which the × buttons under the map set: at true scale, across 500 km of country, a 300 m traffic circuit is a third of a pixel tall and every box here is two rings on top of each other. ×1 is one press away, and the limits in each label are the real ones whichever setting you are on. The 37 that run above 4 km are cut off at a dashed lid, which is a cap and not their ceiling; the label says how high they go.
Czech local time. Aerodrome hours are published for 68 of the 82 aerodromes and for none of the 74 ultralight strips, and nothing else on this map carries hours at all — so this hides part of one layer, not the map. Outside published hours is not “closed”: almost every field adds “otherwise on request”, and a tow launch needs no published hour.
Airfield layer for XCTrackAerodrome zones and traffic circuits XCTrack and XContest leave out (OpenAir · 82 zones, 206 circuits at 157 fields · 208 KB). Not a full airspace set: load it alongside your usual airspace, never instead of it. Import under Preferences → Airspaces and obstacles → Files → Import OpenAir files, or copy it into the XCTrack/Airspaces folder. Provided with no guarantee — it may be out of date or wrong; you are responsible for the airspace you fly in.Download

Aerodrome zones on the map — openAIP's. The download's are this site's own: 82 public aerodromes, 5 500 m radius, ground to 4 000 ft (the AIP calls these ATZ), 15 clipped by an overlying CTR or TMA; positions corrected by 108 m. An ultralight strip has no zone of its own, so those 74 fields carry only their traffic circuitmap: openAIP — CC BY-NC 4.0; download: ŘLP ČR — UAS zones, LKR315A, LKR315BopenAIP 2026-10-05; 2026-10-01
Traffic circuits (okruhy) — drawn by this tool, not a published boundary. Shape scaled off the AIP's VOC charts (±10%); altitude published where stated, otherwise 1 000 ft above the field (measured mean 993 ft over five, spread 820–1 150). At an SLZ strip the runway itself is reconstructed from the reference point and a heading rounded to 10°, so those are marked estcircuit drawn from the VOC charts, altitudes and runway tables from the AIP VFR manual, thresholds from OurAirports—
